new_entities.name: Rhodiola rosea extract
new_entities.description: Standardized Rhodiola rosea extract marketed as an adaptogenic supplement for stress and fatigue.

new_entities.name: Mental fatigue
new_entities.description: Subjective and task-based cognitive fatigue during sustained work, stress, or shift-related exertion.

edges.population: healthy but stressed or shift-working adults
edges.mechanism: Rhodiola is proposed to alter monoaminergic signaling and stress-system reactivity in ways that might preserve attention and reduce perceived fatigue under load. Human data remain inconsistent, suggesting any anti-fatigue effect is contingent on context, extract, and study design rather than robustly reproducible across populations.
edges.summary: Rhodiola rosea does not support a clean pro-performance or anti-fatigue claim. Early physician and stress-related-fatigue trials reported benefits, but a later randomized study in shift-working nursing students found worse fatigue outcomes than placebo, leaving the overall evidence mixed and low confidence.
edges.caveats: The literature is small, uses different fatigue constructs, and often centers on one proprietary extract family. This is a classic case where the marketing narrative is much simpler than the actual trial record.

evidence.notes: Rhodiola rosea in stress induced fatigue--a double blind cross-over study of a standardized extract SHR-5 with a repeated low-dose regimen on the mental performance of healthy physicians during night duty.

evidence.citation: Olsson EM et al 2009 Planta Med
evidence.notes: A randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group study of the standardised extract shr-5 of the roots of Rhodiola rosea in the treatment of subjects with stress-related fatigue.

evidence.citation: Punja S et al 2014 PLoS One
evidence.notes: Rhodiola rosea for mental and physical fatigue in nursing students: a randomized controlled trial.
